adCopy: If you have a litter box in your home you need to know what it’s putting into your air because it’s not just a smell. What your litter box releases into your home every single day is an actual toxic gas that the EPA classifies as a respiratory irritant and you are breathing it right now whether you can smell it or not. I have a cat named Rue. She’s 5, I adopted her during a really rough patch in my life and she has been the best decision I’ve made in years. Her litter box was in the closet in my hallway, I scooped it every day, sometimes twice if I was home. My apartment was clean and I stayed on top of it. For about 8 months I had been getting these headaches a few times a week, usually in the evenings when I was home for the night. I was also waking up stuffy some mornings, not sick just this congestion that would take a couple hours to clear. And I was tired in a way that didn’t match my life, like I should have had more energy than I did but every evening I just felt drained for no reason. I went through the usual routine, tried Zyrtec for a while, did Flonase for a couple months, bought a HEPA purifier and ran it in my hallway every day. I even changed my pillows and my laundry detergent because I was grasping at anything. Nothing changed because I was treating problems I didn’t have while the actual cause sat in my hallway closet doing its thing 24 hours a day. I found out what was really going on because my friend Val who also has cats sent me an article one night about ammonia gas in homes with litter boxes and said “have you seen this because it freaked me out” and I opened it thinking it was going to be some overblown clickbait and it wasn’t. Cat urine contains extremely high concentrations of urea which starts breaking down into ammonia gas the moment it contacts litter. A real toxic airborne chemical the EPA classifies as a respiratory irritant that causes inflammation and irritation to your airways with prolonged exposure. Every time Rue used her box ammonia gas started releasing into my hallway immediately, drifting through the closet door, spreading into the kitchen, getting pulled through my vents, circulating through every room I live and sleep and breathe in. And it never stops because she uses the box multiple times a day so the ammonia is constantly being replenished and constantly building in concentration. And you will never know it’s there because your nose adapts to it within days. You catch the spike when your cat first goes, you scoop it, the strong smell fades, and you think that’s handled. It’s not handled, the ammonia that released during the hours between scoops is already airborne, already in your rooms, already in your vents. Your nose just stopped flagging the constant low level presence because your brain decided that’s just what your home smells like and shut off the alarm. But your lungs don’t shut off. Your sinuses don’t shut off. Your throat doesn’t shut off. They keep reacting to a chemical your nose told you isn’t there anymore and the inflammation builds so slowly you blame allergies or stress or getting older before you ever think to blame the air you’re breathing inside your own home. That’s exactly what I did for 8 months. Headaches, congestion, fatigue, and I blamed everything except the closet in my hallway that was filling my home with a toxic gas while I slept 10 feet away from it. And the worst part was the ammonia gas was just part of it. Cat feces carry Toxoplasma gondii, a parasite the CDC considers 1 of the leading causes of death from foodborne illness in the United States and most people who have it don’t even know. It becomes airborne in microscopic particles every time you scoop, every time your cat digs around in the litter, every time dry particles shift and lift into the air. Cat feces also carry roundworm eggs, hookworm larvae, and giardia, organisms that survive in dry litter for weeks and attach to dust particles and travel through your air into every room. I had been scooping that box every single day with my face right above the litter breathing in whatever was coming off the surface and then spending the rest of my day in a sealed apartment where all of it recirculated through my vents over and over. And the HEPA purifier I was running was completely pointless against the ammonia because ammonia is a gas molecule roughly 1,000 times smaller than what a HEPA filter can catch. It passes right through the filter material like it’s not even there. I was running a machine that collected cat hair while the actual toxic gas floated straight past it into my lungs. Scooping doesn’t remove ammonia from the air, it removes waste from the box but the gas is already airborne. Air fresheners spray perfume on top of a toxic gas so you inhale both. Scented litter does the same. Baking soda and charcoal bags can’t interact with gas molecules circulating through your ductwork. Every product I had tried was designed for what you can see and smell and nothing was built to eliminate the invisible gas that was actually causing my symptoms. I was scared after reading all this but I was determined to not give up Rue. She is the reason my home feels like a home and I wasn’t going to let this be the reason I lose her. But I also wasn’t going to keep breathing a toxic gas every night knowing what I know now so I needed to find something that actually eliminates ammonia gas not filters it, not masks it, eliminates it. I spent the rest of that night going through everything I could find. Most of it was the same useless stuff I already owned. I was getting frustrated because everything being sold to cat owners is designed to deal with the litter and the smell and none of it addresses the gas in the air which is the actual thing causing the damage. Then I came across a thread where a woman described going through the exact same thing I was going through, headaches, and congestion but nothing working. She mentioned a new device called LitterClear. This was something I never heard off or saw because it wasn’t sold in person. That was the only thing that actually made a difference. She said it uses Nano Ion Technology to generate millions of reactive ions that bond to ammonia and VOC molecules in the air and break them apart at the molecular level, converts them into harmless compounds so the gas just doesn’t exist in your air anymore. No filter to trap it, no scent to cover it, it destroys the gas itself. No filters to replace, no maintenance, you plug it in and it runs. That evening I didn’t get a headache and I remember thinking about it specifically because by 8 PM most nights that week I would have already taken ibuprofen and I hadn’t. Within the first week the morning congestion had pretty much stopped and the headaches went from a few times a week to not at all. When Rue used the box I noticed the smell that usually lingered for a while after was gone within minutes instead of hanging around. I ordered a 3rd unit for the hallway near my vent return because I wanted the gas caught before it could distribute through the system. EDIT: It’s been about 3 months. The headaches are gone, the congestion is gone, the fatigue is gone. I feel like I got my apartment back. Val texts me every couple weeks asking if it’s still working and I tell her the same thing every time, my apartment smells like nothing and I feel better at home than I have in over a year. Rue is still here, still on the couch with me every night, and I didn’t have to make a single change to my life except plug in 3 small devices that actually address the thing that was making me sick instead of covering it up. I've spent $3,412 on neck gadgets from Facebook ads. An EMS massager. A TENS unit. A door hammock. A neck stretcher. I have cervical stenosis. Last Saturday my wife made me sell all of it in our driveway. Last Saturday my wife Tina set up two folding tables at the end of our driveway. She covered them with a bedsheet. Then she brought out everything from the hall closet. And she made me price it. An EMS neck massager. The one with the little metal pads that zap you. I paid $189. I put a piece of masking tape on it that said $10. A TENS unit. Still had the sticky pads stuck to the box. Paid $89. Five bucks. A neck hammock that hangs off the top of a door. Paid $59. Five bucks. A blow up neck stretcher collar from Amazon. A massage gun. An acupressure mat with all the little plastic spikes. A red light wand. A posture correcting shirt that zipped up the back. Magnetic patches. Three different contour pillows. A neck cloud. Two kinds of CBD roll on. I lined it all up on the bedsheet like a crime scene. Tina had added it up the night before, sitting at the kitchen table with a highlighter and a year of credit card statements. $3,412. That's not counting the chiropractor. That's not counting the epidurals. That's just the stuff I bought from ads at one in the morning. People started pulling up around 8. Our neighbor Carol picked up the posture shirt and held it up and said, "Greg, is this yours?" I said yeah, Carol. It's mine. I'm 49. I've been a mechanic for twenty six years. Twenty six years of lying on a creeper under cars with my head tilted back. Or bent over an engine bay with my chin on my chest. Every mechanic I know has a bad neck. You just deal with it. I dealt with it until I couldn't. Two years ago I got an MRI. Cervical stenosis. Moderate. C5 and C6. Bone spurs. Narrowing. The spine guy looked at it and said, "You may need surgery someday. But not yet. Try some PT. Come back if your hands go numb." So I did PT. Helped for an hour. I did the chiropractor. Three times a week for two months. Felt great walking out. Gone by dinner. Eleven hundred dollars. Two epidurals. The first one gave me twelve good days. The second gave me five. And every single day, my neck was tight. Not sore. Tight. Like a rope somebody keeps cranking. A rock in my left trap I could feel the edges of. A burn inside my shoulder blade like a hot nail under the skin. A headache sitting behind my left eye by 3pm. And my neck ground like gravel when I turned it. The guys in the shop could hear it over the air tools. That's when the ads started. I don't know how they knew. I'd google "cervical stenosis" one night and the next night my whole Facebook was neck stuff. "Doctors are stunned by this neck device." "Chiropractors hate this." "Finally, relief for spinal stenosis without surgery." And it was always at night. Always when I was lying there at 1am with my neck on fire and nothing else to do but scroll. So I bought one. The EMS massager came first. You hang it around your neck and it sends little shocks through those pads. My skin twitched like a frog in science class. It felt like something for about twenty minutes. Then it felt like nothing. The TENS unit was next. Same idea, sticky pads, a little box with a dial. It buzzed. The pain got kind of fuzzy for half an hour. Then the pads lost their stick and it was back. The door hammock was the one I really believed in. You hook it over the top of a door, put your head in the sling, and lean back so it pulls on your neck. It felt amazing for about five minutes. Then I stood up, and it was gone before I got to the couch. The third time I used it, my neck went into a spasm so bad I had to call in sick the next day. The massage gun I used until Tina took it away. Said I was beating myself up. The pillows were all the same. Great for one night, and then I was back to two pillows, no pillow, a rolled up towel. Fourteen of them in a year. And here's the part I'm not proud of. After the eighth or ninth package, Tina stopped asking what it was. She'd just see the box on the porch and look at me. So I started having them shipped to the shop. I'd sneak them home in the truck. Stick them in the closet. Try them when she was asleep. I was a 49 year old man hiding neck gadgets from his wife. Then one Sunday she was doing the bills and found a receipt for the fourteenth one. Shipped to the shop. I figured she'd be mad. She wasn't. She cried. "Greg, I'm not upset about the money," she said. "I'm scared. You keep buying these things because you're scared. And I keep watching them not work. What happens when there's nothing left to try?" I didn't have an answer. Because I knew what was left. Some days my fingers tingle when I'm under a car, holding a wrench up over my head. And every time, my stomach drops. Is this it? Is this the numbness he meant? Because when the gadgets run out, there's only one thing left to try. And that's the surgeon's table. The collar. The plate in your neck. Four months out of the shop. I've got a mortgage. A kid starting at the community college. A boss who's been real patient. I lay there that night doing the math. And then I did something worse. I scrolled. Looking for the next one. That's when Tina said, "We're having a garage sale. All of it goes." So there I was on Saturday morning. Standing in my own driveway, selling three thousand dollars of failure for five bucks apiece. Around 10, an old guy in a ball cap and a Carhartt jacket walked up. Seventy something. Big hands. He picked up the TENS unit and turned it over. "How much?" "Five bucks. I paid eighty nine." He laughed. "I paid ninety nine for mine." Then he looked at me. I had my hand dug into my left trap. I didn't even know it was there. My hand just goes there now. "Stenosis?" he said. I about dropped my coffee. "How do you know that?" "Because I've got it too. C4 to C6. Fifteen years now." He pointed at my hand. "I know that hand. I did that for ten years before I figured anything out." He set the TENS unit down. Looked over the whole table. "I had all this," he said. "Every bit of it. The zapper. The hammock. Those pillows. My wife made me haul it to the dump." His name was Hank. 73. Retired lineman. Forty one years up on power poles with his head tilted back. "Does any of it actually work?" I said. It came out quieter than I meant. "Some of it did something," he said. "That's the trap. Every one of these worked for twenty minutes. That's why you kept buying the next one." "Then why does it always come back?" He leaned on the table. "Because it's not just the bone, son. When something's narrowed in your neck, all the muscles around it clamp down to protect it. Your traps. The base of your skull. Along your shoulder blade. That's your rock. That's the burn." "And they don't clamp down once. They clamp down every single day. Because the reason they're guarding is still sitting there." He tapped the TENS unit. "So this buzzes your skin for half an hour. That hammock yanks on you for five minutes. The chiropractor cracks you three times a week. And every one of them gets those muscles to let go. Once." "Then they clamp right back down. And you go buy the next thing." I stood there looking at fourteen boxes. "You didn't buy junk," he said. "Well. Some of it's junk. But mostly you bought things you'd use twice and stick in a closet. And you can't beat something that comes back every day with something you use twice." Fourteen gadgets. Every one of them worked. For twenty minutes. For a night. For twelve days. The relief was never the problem. How often I got it was. Then he said the thing I still think about. "And every day you don't let those muscles go, they win another one. I lost ten years like that. Ten years of buying the next thing and sitting in my recliner. I missed my granddaughter's whole first season of softball because I couldn't sit on the bleachers. Don't do what I did." "So what do you do?" I said. He sighed like he knew exactly how this was going to sound. "I know. You don't want to hear about one more neck thing." "I really don't." "That's fair," he said. "I'm three houses down, the blue one with the boat. Come by tonight. I'll show you mine. You don't have to buy anything." I almost didn't go. Tina made me. Hank's wife answered the door and pointed me to the living room. On the couch was a gray, curved cushion with a raised ridge down the middle and a little round orange panel of buttons on one end. A tag on the side said Lanarie Atlas Relief. "That's it?" I said. "That's another one." "Yeah," Hank said. "But it's the only one I ever bought that I still use every day. Fifteen years of junk and this is the one." "What's different about it?" "Everything else did one thing. Buzzed you. Pounded you. Hung you off a door. This one you lie back on. That curve goes right under the base of your skull. It heats up right there. It vibrates on the knots. And it slowly fills with air and stretches your neck out a little, so it's not holding your head up for once." "Fifteen minutes in the morning. Fifteen at night. Every day. Because the tightness is every day." "Start it on low," he said. "And with your stenosis, run it by your doctor. Mine said go ahead." "Lie down," he said. "Go on." I lay down on a stranger's couch and felt like an idiot. He set the heat on low. The first thing I noticed was I wasn't holding my head up. That sounds stupid. But I didn't know I was always doing it. Even lying down. Even on a pillow. Some part of my neck was always on the clock. Then the warmth came in. Right at the base of my skull. Deeper than any heating pad, because I was lying on it instead of having it draped over me. Then the vibration found the rock in my left trap. It didn't hammer on it like that massage gun. It just hummed into it. Then it started to fill with air. Slow. And I felt my neck stretch out a little. Like somebody took the weight of my head and held it for me. About ten minutes in, my left shoulder came down. I didn't push it down. It just dropped away from my ear on its own. I didn't even know it had been up there. When it clicked off, I sat up and turned my head. Still a little grind. But that hot nail in my shoulder blade was quiet. Don't get excited, I told myself. You've been here fourteen times. Everything works for twenty minutes. I went home and didn't say a word to Tina. The next morning I was under a Silverado by 7:30. At lunch, I realized I hadn't reached for my trap all morning. I went back to Hank's that night and used it again. Then I went home and looked it up. And I'll tell you the first thing I read. Not the features. The guarantee. 90 days. Money back. I'd bought fourteen neck gadgets and I'd never once gotten a dollar back. I read it three times. Then I ordered one. And for the first time in a year, I had it shipped to the house. Tina saw the box on the porch. She looked at me. I said, "This one comes with a money back guarantee. And Hank down the street has used his every day for three years." She didn't say anything. But she didn't roll her eyes either. Every morning before work. Every night before bed. Fifteen minutes. I set an alarm on my phone like it was a service appointment. The first week, I slept through the night three times. The second week, I stopped carrying Tylenol in my toolbox. The third week was the one I watched. Because that's always when everything quit on me. The chiropractor. The epidurals. Every gadget. Right around week three. It held. Then deer season. Five days at hunting camp with my brother. I left it at home. Figured I'd be fine. By the third day, the rock was back. By the fourth, I couldn't turn my head to look through the scope without turning my whole body. And on the drive home, my fingers started tingling on the steering wheel. That's when I really got what Hank meant. It doesn't fix my stenosis. Nothing I lie on is going to do that. It just lets go of the muscles that clamp down around it. Every single day. And the second I skip, they clamp right back down. It never stopped working. I stopped using it. I haven't missed a day since. I bought a second one for the shop. I still have stenosis. I might still need surgery someday. I'm not going to pretend I won't. But it doesn't run my life anymore. And I'm done losing years to it. It's been five months. No packages on the porch. No boxes hidden in the truck. I haven't clicked on a single neck ad. Last month Tina was doing the bills. She looked up from the statements and said, "Greg. What's different with you?" I said I figured some stuff out. She smiled and went back to the bills. We had another garage sale in the spring. Mostly the kid's old stuff. There was one thing left over from the first one. That door hammock. Nobody wanted it. A guy in his thirties, construction boots, picked it up. He was rubbing the back of his neck with his other hand. I looked at him. "Stenosis?" I said. He about dropped it. Here's what I wish somebody had told me before I spent $3,412. When something's wrong in your neck, the muscles around it clamp down to protect it. Every single day. So you have to let them go every single day too. Not with a gadget you use twice. Not with something that buzzes your skin for twenty minutes. Every day. Because every day you don't is a day they win. And you don't get those days back. If you've bought the EMS massager, the TENS unit, the door hammock or the neck stretcher. If your closet has more pillows in it than your bed. If every single thing worked for one night, and then you were back to scrolling at 1am. If you've started hiding packages. If your fingers tingle and you wonder if you're running out of things to try before the surgeon's table. And if you're just tired of being the sucker who keeps hoping. I was you. For two years. adCopy: ⭐☆☆☆☆ — One star. I put this on for a headache at 2 PM. I woke up at 5:10. Dinner wasn't started.... I need you to understand how insulting this is. I have not taken an accidental nap since 2013. I have not slept through a whole night since about then either. I'm 58. I work part-time from home doing bookkeeping for my brother-in-law's landscaping company, which is its own kind of headache, and for twelve years my body has had exactly two settings. Tired. And wide awake. Never asleep. Tired all day, then the minute I lie down at night, my brain opens a spreadsheet. Invoices. My mother's appointments. The noise the car is making. The thing I said to my neighbor in August that I'm still not sure came out right. I'd lie there until 1, 2 in the morning. Then I'd wake up at 4:30 and that was it. Done. Ready or not. I tried all of it. Melatonin. Magnesium. CBD gummies from my cousin's friend. Sleepy tea. A meditation app. Earplugs. A weighted blanket that made me feel like I was being held down by a golden retriever. Then the prescriptions. Ambien, until it stopped working. Then trazodone, which gave me a fog so thick I once drove to the pharmacy and forgot why. It was taking more than sleep from me. I made a mistake on a payroll run in June that cost my brother-in-law an awkward phone call with two of his guys. I'd never made a mistake like that in my life. I started dreading Sunday nights because Monday meant numbers, and I didn't trust my own head with numbers anymore. I'd snap at my husband for chewing too loud. I cried at a Subaru commercial. My husband said, "You're not yourself lately." He was right. I wasn't. I was a tired, short-fused stranger wearing my clothes. So when my sister gave me this mask for my birthday, I put it in the closet. Another gadget. I had a drawer full of them. A cheap eye mask, a jade roller I used twice, a white noise machine still in the box. Then one Tuesday in October, I had one of those tension headaches that starts in your jaw and crawls up behind your eyes. Too many invoices. I remembered the mask. I figured some warmth over my eyes couldn't hurt. It was 2:04 PM. I know because I had just checked the clock. I put it on. I pressed the button. Warmth first, around my eyes and temples. Then this slow, gentle squeeze at my temples, letting go, squeezing again. Like somebody's hands. Not buzzing. Slow. My jaw let go. I remember that. My shoulders dropped. And then it was 5:10. FIVE TEN. The mask was in my lap. My phone had two missed calls from my sister and a text from my husband that said, "Are you alive? Car's here, house is dark." The chicken was still in the freezer. I don't even know if the headache went away, because I was unconscious. I called my sister back and told her I was very upset with her gift. She said, "You slept? In the DAYTIME? You?" She was more shocked than I was. That night I put it on at bed. 10:30. I didn't see 10:45. I want you to understand what that meant to me. For twelve years, bedtime had been a negotiation. I'd stall. I'd fold laundry that didn't need folding. I'd scroll my phone in the kitchen with the lights off, because if I got into bed too early I'd just lie there longer. My husband used to say I went to bed like I was walking into a dentist's office. That night, I got into bed, put the mask on, felt the warmth start around my eyes, felt that slow squeeze at my temples, and the next thing I knew the birds were going and my husband was asking if I wanted coffee. I cried a little in the shower that morning. Not sad crying. The other kind. The kind where something you'd given up on turns out to still be possible. I still wake up some nights, around 3, the way I always did. The difference now is I put it back on, press the button and let it do its thing. Most of the time I don't remember it turning off. Here's why that happened, because I went and read up on it the next morning like a lunatic. When you've been stressed for years, your body gets stuck in fight-or-flight. Heart a little fast. Jaw clenched. Stress hormones running when they're supposed to be off. Cortisol, your alert hormone, is supposed to be at its lowest at night. When you're stuck on alert, it isn't. So you're exhausted, but your body won't let you go under, because as far as it's concerned, there's danger. The racing mind isn't the problem. It's the alarm. That's also why the pills kept failing me. They don't turn the alarm off. They sedate you over the top of it. Sedation isn't rest. Your body adapts, the dose creeps up, and when it wears off, the alarm comes back louder. That's called rebound insomnia. What your body needs is the signal that it's safe. You can't think your way there. But your body responds to physical signals: warmth, darkness and slow, steady pressure. That's your vagus nerve, your body's off switch. Massage studies have found cortisol, the stress hormone, drops by an average of 31%. It's how you settle a newborn. Warm, snug, dark. Nobody hands a crying baby a pill. That's exactly what this mask does. Warmth. A slow air-pressure massage around your eyes and temples. Total darkness. It turns itself off after about 15 minutes, so nothing runs all night. Not sedation. Reset. It's been five weeks. I still wake up some nights, but I fall back asleep. I'm getting close to seven hours most nights. I didn't change anything else. Same routine, same everything my doctor has me on. I've also learned my lesson. I no longer use it before 5 PM unless I'm willing to lose the afternoon. And now I have new problems. I fell asleep on the couch at 8:30 last Thursday and missed the end of my show. My husband refuses to tell me who did it. My sister keeps "forgetting" to give it back when she visits.
